Problem 1

A metal ball of radius $r_1 = 10\,\mathrm{cm}$ is surrounded by a metal spherical shell, concentric with it, of inner radius $r_2 = 2r_1$ (see Fig. 1). There is a vacuum between the shell and the ball. The ball is coated with a thin, uniform layer of the curium isotope ${}^{242}\mathrm{Cm}$ in the amount $n = 0.01$ mol. The ${}^{242}\mathrm{Cm}$ nucleus decays by emitting an alpha particle of energy $E_0 \approx 6.1\,\mathrm{MeV}$. The half-life of curium is $t_{1/2} = 163$ days. The shell is connected to the ball by a thin wire running radially. We assume that the presence of the wire and the current flowing in it do not affect the electric field between the shells. The alpha particles are completely absorbed by the shell and by the ball, but they are neither absorbed nor scattered by the curium.

a) What is the current flowing in the wire if its resistance is equal to $R_1 = 100\,\mathrm{k\Omega}$?

b) What should the resistance $R_2$ of the wire be so that the current flowing in it is equal to half of the current determined in part a)?

Avogadro number $N_{\mathrm{A}} \approx 6.0\cdot10^{23}\,\mathrm{mol^{-1}}$, magnitude of the electron charge $e \approx 1.6\cdot10^{-19}\,\mathrm{C}$. We neglect the emission of electrons from the ball and from the shell surrounding it.

We consider the stationary situation, i.e. after the current in the wire has (approximately) settled, over a time short compared with $t_{1/2}$.

Problem 2

A rod of length $l$ and mass $m$ has been placed on an inclined plane with angle of inclination $\alpha$ (see Fig. 2), at a height $h$ above the floor (where $h \gg l$).

a) Describe qualitatively the motion of the rod.

b) Determine the velocity of the rod in the last phase of the motion. Give the numerical value for $h = 6.4\,\mathrm{m}$, $\alpha = 45^\circ$, $g = 10\,\mathrm{m/s^2}$ (gravitational acceleration).

Friction and air resistance are neglected. The rod is perfectly rigid and all the time lies in a vertical plane perpendicular to the surface of the inclined plane. The floor and the inclined plane absorb impacts perfectly, i.e. they cause the velocity component perpendicular to them of the striking point to be equal to 0 just after the impact, and their deflection during the impact is negligibly small.

The moment of inertia of the rod about its centre of mass is equal to $I = (1/12)ml^2$. At the initial moment the rod was at rest. The angle of inclination satisfies the condition $0^\circ < \alpha < 90^\circ$, where $\alpha$ is not close to $90^\circ$.

problems.title: Problem 1
problems.problem:
Problem 1

A ball strikes a horizontal floor at an angle $\alpha$ with velocity $v_0$. The coefficient of friction between the ball and the floor is equal to $\mu$. At what distance from the place of the first impact will the ball strike the floor again?

Give the numerical values for $\alpha = 45^\circ$, $v_0 = 10\,\mathrm{m/s}$ in two cases: $\mu = 0.1$ and $\mu = 0.8$.

The ball does not rotate before the collision. The duration of the collision is very short, and during the collision the deformation of the ball is negligibly small compared with its radius. The ball is perfectly elastic, i.e. in the case when, not rotating, it strikes the floor vertically, the collision is perfectly elastic. The thickness of the ball's shell is very small compared with the radius. The shell does not undergo tangential deformation. The mass of the air in the ball is negligibly small compared with the mass of its shell. Neglect aerodynamic drag.

Gravitational acceleration $g \approx 9.8\,\mathrm{m/s^2}$, and the moment of inertia of a sphere of radius $R$ and mass $m$ about an axis passing through its centre is $I = (2/3)mR^2$.

Problem 2

A spherical vessel consists of concentric, thin, metal spheres of radii $r_2$ and $r_1$ (where $r_2 > r_1$), between which there is a vacuum (see the figure). The outer sphere is divided by a plane into two parts, the smaller of which has area $S_3$. A mixture of water of mass $m_W$ and ice of mass $m_L$ has been placed in the inner sphere. The larger part of the outer shell of the vessel has a constant temperature $t_2$, and the smaller part a constant temperature $t_3$ ($t_2$ and $t_3$ are temperatures on the Celsius scale).

After what time will the ice melt completely?

Give the numerical result for $r_1 = 0.04\,\mathrm{m}$, $r_2 = 0.08\,\mathrm{m}$, $S_3 = 0.03\,\mathrm{m^2}$, $m_W = 0.1\,\mathrm{kg}$, $m_L = 0.1\,\mathrm{kg}$, $t_2 = 20\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$, $t_3 = 10\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$.

The surfaces of the spheres are perfectly black. The heat capacity of the vessel can be neglected. Assume that the ice is all the time in thermodynamic equilibrium with the water. The pressure inside the inner sphere is all the time equal to normal pressure.

The heat of fusion of ice is $q = 334\,\mathrm{kJ/kg}$, the Stefan–Boltzmann constant $\sigma = 5.7\cdot10^{-8}\,\mathrm{W\cdot m^{-2}\cdot K^{-4}}$, the specific heat of water $c_W = 4.2\,\mathrm{kJ\cdot kg^{-1}\cdot K^{-1}}$, the specific heat of ice $c_L = 2.1\,\mathrm{kJ\cdot kg^{-1}\cdot K^{-1}}$, the melting point of ice under normal conditions $T_0 = 273.15\,\mathrm{K}$.

Problem 1

On a horizontal plane there is a uniform, thin, initially stationary disc of radius $R$ and mass $M$. At the moment $t_0 = 0$ a small projectile of mass $m$ is fired with velocity $v$ from a point P on this plane, at a distance $d$ from the centre S of the disc. The projectile slides on the plane, then strikes the disc and sticks to it at the point of collision, at a distance $a$ from the axis PS (Fig. 1). There is no friction between the plane and the disc, nor between the plane and the projectile.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/physics-olympiads-bank/main/images/poland-2008-1-fig1.png

Fig. 1. The disc and the projectile – top view.

After what smallest time $t > 0$ should the second shot be fired so that the second projectile hits the disc at the place where the first projectile struck? The second shot is fired with an identical projectile, from the same place, in the same direction and with the same initial velocity as the first.

Give the numerical result for $M = 100\,\mathrm{g}$, $m = 10\,\mathrm{g}$, $R = 0.05\,\mathrm{m}$, $a = 0.04\,\mathrm{m}$, $v = 10\,\mathrm{m/s}$, $d = 2\,\mathrm{m}$.

The moment of inertia of the disc about its axis of rotational symmetry is $I_0 = MR^2/2$.

problems.title: Problem 2
problems.problem:
Problem 2

Consider the following model of an optical fibre (a so-called multimode fibre): a cylindrical core of radius $r = 25\,\mathrm{\mu m}$ and refractive index $n_1 = 1.475$ is surrounded by a cladding (whose thickness does not matter for the behaviour of the fibre) of refractive index $n_2 = 1.460$.

At a distance $d = 25\,\mathrm{\mu m}$ from the beginning of the fibre, a point-like, isotropic source of electromagnetic radiation of power $P = 1\,\mathrm{mW}$, emitting radiation of wavelength $1.55\,\mathrm{\mu m}$, has been placed on its axis of symmetry (Fig. 2).

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/physics-olympiads-bank/main/images/poland-2008-2-fig1.png

Fig. 2. The optical fibre and the radiation source.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/physics-olympiads-bank/main/images/poland-2008-2-fig2.png

Fig. 3. The signal corresponding to the sequence 0110101001.

[Label in Fig. 3: natezenie sygnalu (natężenie sygnału) = signal intensity.]

Calculate the maximum distance $L$ over which information can be transmitted through this fibre at a rate $S$ equal to a) 1 Gb/s, b) 1 Mb/s, c) 1 kb/s, where b/s denotes bit/second.

Take into account that:

• The attenuation coefficient $\alpha$, defined as

$$\alpha = (10/L)\log_{10}\left(E_{out}/E_{in}\right)$$

where $E_{out}$ is the energy of the signal after travelling the distance $L$ if at the input its energy was $E_{in}$, is in the case of the core equal to $\alpha = -0.02/\mathrm{km}$.

• The detector registering a pulse at the end of the fibre is able to register pulses of energy greater than $E_d = 10^{-15}\,\mathrm{J}$.

• A single pulse (bit) initially has the shape of a rectangle of width $1/S$ (by width we mean here the time interval between the beginning and the end of sending this pulse – Fig. 3).

We consider that information cannot be transmitted if, as a result of the transmission, the duration of a single pulse increases more than twofold.

• The parameters in the problem are chosen so that the wave nature of the radiation can be neglected and it can be treated as a beam of rays.

• Radiation that finds itself in the cladding is attenuated so quickly that its role in the transmission of information can be neglected.

• The radiation source is placed in air (assume that the refractive index is $n = 1$), and the reflection at the air–core boundary can be neglected.

• The speed of light in vacuum is $c \approx 3\cdot10^{8}\,\mathrm{m/s}$.

problems.title: Problem 3
problems.problem:
Problem 3

Thermal energy is transmitted from a combined heat and power plant by means of a straight metal pipe inside which hot water flows. The pipe runs at a depth $h$ below the surface of the ground, at a distance $d$ from a channel filled with water, parallel to it (Fig. 4). It is known that the temperature of the ground just below the surface, exactly above the pipe, is $t_p$, and the temperature of the water and of the ground in contact with it is $t_b$.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/physics-olympiads-bank/main/images/poland-2008-3-fig1.png

Fig. 4. A heating pipe in the ground.

[Labels in the figure: powietrze = air; rura = pipe; woda = water; ziemia = ground.]

a) Calculate the rate of heat loss per unit length of the pipe, i.e. the amount of heat flowing into the ground per unit time from a section of the pipe of unit length.

b) Knowing that the radius of the pipe is $R$, calculate its temperature.

In parts a) and b) give the numerical results for $h = 3\,\mathrm{m}$, $d = 2\,\mathrm{m}$, $t_p = 10^\circ\mathrm{C}$, $t_b = 4^\circ\mathrm{C}$, $R = 0.1\,\mathrm{m}$, thermal conductivity of the ground $\sigma = 0.7\,\mathrm{W/(m\cdot K)}$.

Make the following simplifying assumptions:

• the surface of the ground is flat and horizontal; no heat flows through it (i.e. we assume that air is a thermal insulator);

• the channel has infinite depth and is filled with water up to the surface of the ground; its edge is vertical and at every point has the temperature $t_b$;

• the ground is homogeneous; its temperature at any place does not change in time;

• the diameter of the pipe is small compared with $h$ and $d$, and its temperature is constant;

• there is no transport of energy by radiation.

The thermal conductivity $\sigma$ is defined as follows: consider two close parallel surfaces, a distance $\Delta r$ apart, each of area $S$. The region between them is filled with a medium of thermal conductivity $\sigma$. If the temperature on one of these surfaces is $t$, and on the other $t + \Delta t$, then the flux of thermal energy (heat per unit time) flowing perpendicularly to them is equal to $J_S = S\sigma\,\Delta t/\Delta r$.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/physics-olympiads-bank/main/images/poland-2009-1-fig1.png

Determine the maximum value of the velocity $v_{\max}$ at which the pipe rolls without slipping on the table, touching it at more than one point. Discuss the dependence of the obtained result on $L$ at fixed values of $q/m$, $R$, $\mu$ and $g$.

Problem 3 [20 points]

Consider a loop of wire loaded with a weight of mass $m$ (see the figure), located in surroundings at temperature $T_0$. The ends of the loop are connected to a voltage $U$.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/physics-olympiads-bank/main/images/poland-2009-3-fig1.png

When the length of the wire is $l$ and its temperature is $T$, the electrical resistance of the loop is equal to $R = R_0\left[1 + G\left(l - l_0\right)/l_0 + a_R\left(T - T_0\right)\right]$, where $G$, $a_R$, $R_0$, $l_0$ are constants, while the tension force of the wire is $F_N = k\left\{l - l_0\left[1 + \alpha\left(T - T_0\right)\right]\right\}$, where $k$ is the elastic constant and $\alpha$ is the coefficient of linear expansion. It is known that in the situation considered the thermal power $P_c$ carried away from the wire to the surroundings satisfies the relation $P_c = \beta\cdot\left(T - T_0\right)$, where $\beta$ is a positive constant. Neglecting the heat capacity of the wire, determine the frequency of small vertical oscillations of the weight on the loop.

Give the numerical value of this frequency for $k = 5000\,\mathrm{N/m}$, $l_0 = 1\,\mathrm{m}$, $m = 1\,\mathrm{kg}$, $U = 2\,\mathrm{V}$, $R_0 = 2\,\Omega$, $\alpha = 1\cdot10^{-5}\,\mathrm{K^{-1}}$, $\beta = 0.01\,\mathrm{W/K}$, $a_R = 5\cdot10^{-3}\,\mathrm{K^{-1}}$, $T_0 = 300\,\mathrm{K}$ and $G = 200$.

In the calculations restrict yourself to terms linear in the increments of the temperature and of the length of the wire. The mass of the wire is negligible compared with $m$.

Additional information: the phenomenon of a relatively large dependence of the resistance of some materials on their deformation is used in sensors measuring forces (so-called strain gauges). For "ordinary" materials a typical value of the constant $G$ is close to 2.

Problem 1

A spacecraft of mass $m$ orbits the Sun in a circular orbit of radius $R$, where $R \gg r_s$, $r_s$ being the radius of the Sun. The spacecraft is equipped with a foldable space sail which, when unfolded, has area $S$. Initially the sail is folded. By what maximum value $\Delta R$ can the distance of the spacecraft from the Sun be increased before it goes around the Sun twice? Only the sail under consideration may be used for propulsion.

The unfolded sail is flat, reflects electromagnetic radiation perfectly, and is always set perpendicular to the spacecraft–Sun direction. The surface area of the spacecraft together with the folded sail is negligibly small compared with the area of the unfolded sail.

Give the numerical value of $\Delta R$ for

$R = 200\cdot10^{9}\,\mathrm{m}$, $m = 5000\,\mathrm{kg}$, $S = 10^{4}\,\mathrm{m^2}$.

The time of unfolding (and possible folding) of the sail is negligibly small compared with the orbital period of the spacecraft around the Sun. The surface temperature of the Sun is $T_s = 5800\,\mathrm{K}$, the mass of the Sun

$M = 2.0\cdot10^{30}\,\mathrm{kg}$, and its radius $r_s = 7.0\cdot10^{8}\,\mathrm{m}$.

The Stefan–Boltzmann constant is equal to $\sigma = 5.7\cdot10^{-8}\,\mathrm{W/\left(m^2K^4\right)}$, the gravitational constant $G = 6.7\cdot10^{-11}\,\mathrm{m^3/kg\cdot s^2}$, the speed of light $c = 3.0\cdot10^{8}\,\mathrm{m/s}$.

problems.title: Problem 1
problems.problem:
Problem 1 [20 points]

A spherical, perfectly black space probe "Lord Darth Vader" uses the radioactive plutonium isotope ${}^{238}\mathrm{Pu}$ as its power supply. Plutonium of mass $m$ is placed inside the probe in a container whose walls completely absorb the decay products of plutonium. The temperature of the container is equal to $T_1$; the temperature of the other elements of the probe does not change in time.

Assuming that the power $P$ used to operate the probe is produced by an ideal (reversible) heat engine which takes heat from the container with plutonium, calculate this power.

Consider two cases:

a) all the work produced by the engine under consideration is used (after conversion into electrical energy) to power the on-board computers;

b) all the work produced by the engine under consideration is sent outside the probe (e.g. in the form of a laser beam).

The half-life of ${}^{238}\mathrm{Pu}$ is $t_{1/2} = 87.7$ years. Assume that the decay proceeds according to the reaction

$${}^{238}_{94}\mathrm{Pu} \to {}^{234}_{92}\mathrm{U} + {}^{4}_{2}\mathrm{He}$$

and neglect other nuclear reactions. Neglect the radiation reaching the probe from outside. The radius of the probe is $R$.

Give the numerical results for $m = 2\,\mathrm{kg}$, $T_1 = 500\,\mathrm{K}$, $R = 0.5\,\mathrm{m}$.

The atomic masses are $m_{{}^{238}_{94}\mathrm{Pu}} = 238.04955\,\mathrm{u}$, $m_{{}^{234}_{92}\mathrm{U}} = 234.04095\,\mathrm{u}$, $m_{{}^{4}_{2}\mathrm{He}} = 4.00260\,\mathrm{u}$, where $\mathrm{u} = 1.66\cdot10^{-27}\,\mathrm{kg}$.

Stefan–Boltzmann constant $\sigma = 5.67\cdot10^{-8}\,\mathrm{W/\left(m^2K^4\right)}$, speed of light $c = 3.00\cdot10^{8}\,\mathrm{m/s}$.

The tube can rotate freely about its axis but is initially at rest. Give the numerical result for $L = 0.5\,\mathrm{m}$, $r_1 = 0.010\,\mathrm{m}$, $r_2 = 0.009\,\mathrm{m}$, $B_0 = 1\,\mathrm{T}$, $Q = 6\cdot10^{-5}\,\mathrm{C}$, $I = 6\cdot10^{-9}\,\mathrm{kg\cdot m^2}$.

problems.title: Problem 3

Problem 3 [20 points]

A plano-convex lens with radius of curvature $R$ and thickness (on the optical axis) $d$ is made of a material with a refractive index that varies with the distance $r$ from its axis according to the formula

$$n(r) = n_1 + a\cdot r^2,$$

where $n_1$ and $a$ are constants. The refractive index of the medium outside the lens is $n_0$.

a) Consider a ray parallel to the axis of the lens, incident on it from the flat side at a distance $r_1$ from this axis. Describe qualitatively and discuss the further path of the ray.

b) Determine the optical (converging) power of this lens. Assume that $\frac{|\Delta r|}{d} \ll 1$, $\frac{|\Delta r|}{r_1} \ll 1$, where $\Delta r$ is the distance by which a ray parallel to the optical axis of the lens, incident on the flat side of this lens at a distance $r_1$ from the axis, moves away from this axis as a result of passing through the lens. Consider paraxial rays, i.e. assume that $r_1$ is small.

Note: for $|x| \ll 1$, in the linear approximation we have

$$\left(1+x\right)^n \approx 1 + nx, \quad \ln\left(1+x\right) \approx x,$$

where $n$ is any real number.

A conducting tape consists of many identical, parallel, insulated wires. The width $w$ of this tape is much larger than its thickness, and the distance between neighbouring wires and the thickness of the insulation can be neglected.

Then it was folded in the opposite direction through an angle of $180^\mathrm{o}$ along a straight line making an angle of $60^\mathrm{o}$ with the direction of the wires, and this operation was repeated $3n-1$ times in total. The distance between the folds is such that each flat fragment between folds forms an equilateral triangle, called a plate below. The end fragments of the tape were cut off so that equilateral triangles were also formed at the beginning and at the end. As a result, a system of $3n$ parallel fragments in the shape of an equilateral triangle (plates) of height $w$ was formed. The distance between neighbouring plates is $d$ ($d \ll w$).

The ends of the tape were connected to supply leads in such a way that the current of the same intensity flows through every wire forming the tape, i.e. a current of uniform density flows through every plate. The total current is equal to $I$.

Determine the electrodynamic force acting on each of the plates. Neglect the influence of the magnetic field produced by the supply leads. Take the magnetic permeability of the insulation of the wires and the magnetic permeability of air equal to the magnetic permeability of vacuum $\mu_0$.

[Information that may be useful (printed on a separate page for the whole paper):

1. Gauss's law

For the electric field $\vec{E}$ in vacuum, the gravitational field (gravitational acceleration) $\vec{\gamma}$ and the magnetic induction vector $\vec{B}$, the total flux $\varPhi_{\text{całk}}$ of the given field through a closed surface is equal to

$$\varPhi_{\text{całk}} = \begin{cases} \frac{1}{\varepsilon_0}Q & \text{for the electric field,} \\ -4\pi G\cdot M & \text{for the gravitational field,} \\ 0 & \text{for the magnetic field,} \end{cases}$$

where $Q$ is the total electric charge contained inside the surface considered, $M$ the total mass contained inside the surface considered, $\varepsilon_0$ the electric permittivity of vacuum, and $G$ the universal gravitational constant.

$\varepsilon_0 = 8.85\cdot10^{-12}\,\mathrm{F/m}$, $G = 6.67\cdot10^{-11}\,\mathrm{N\cdot m^2/kg^2}$.

2. Magnetic induction of the field produced by a current flowing in a plane

If in the plane $z = 0$ a current of constant linear density $j$ flows along the $x$ axis, in the direction of the axis, then the components of the magnetic induction vector of the field produced by this current are equal to

$$B_y = -\frac{1}{2}\mu_0 j \ \text{ for } z > 0, \quad B_y = +\frac{1}{2}\mu_0 j \ \text{ for } z < 0, \qquad B_x = B_z = 0.$$

The linear density of a current flowing in a plane is the current $I$ flowing in a strip of width $a$ divided by this width, i.e. $j = I/a$.

The above formulas follow from Ampère's law, presented below (in a simplified form).

Ampère's law

The circulation $\mathcal{E}_B$ of the magnetic induction vector $\vec{B}$ along a closed polygonal line W is the quantity

$$\mathcal{E}_B = \sum_{k=1}^{N}\vec{B}_k\cdot\Delta\vec{l}_k,$$

where $\Delta\vec{l}_k$ correspond to the successive segments of the polygonal line W, and $\vec{B}_k$ is the mean magnetic induction vector on the segment $\Delta\bar{l}_k$.

In vacuum, according to Ampère's law, the circulation $\mathcal{E}_B$ of the magnetic induction vector $\vec{B}$ along a closed polygonal line W is equal to the total current $I$ flowing through the surface $S$ whose boundary is the polygonal line W, multiplied by the magnetic permeability of vacuum $\mu_0$:

$$\mathcal{E}_B = \mu_0 I.$$

Problem 1 [20 points]

A uniform ball of mass $m$ and radius $r$ was rolling without slipping with speed $v_0$ on a horizontal surface, and its axis of rotation was horizontal. At a certain moment the ball struck a smooth vertical wall at an angle $\alpha$ and bounced off it elastically. Since the wall was smooth, there was no friction between the ball and the wall. After the bounce the ball slid on the ground for some time, and the kinetic friction occurring then must be taken into account. The coefficient of this friction is $f$. The bounce off the wall lasted much shorter than the sliding of the ball after the bounce. Neglect rolling friction and air resistance.

a) Will the path of the ball after the bounce be straight, curved away from the wall, or curved towards the wall? The attached figure shows the situation from above.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/physics-olympiads-bank/main/images/poland-2023-1-fig1.png

b) Determine the direction and the magnitude of the velocity of the ball after the sliding has stopped.

Notes:

Angular momentum is a vector, and for the ball, relative to its centre of mass, it is equal to

$$\vec{L} = I\vec{\omega},$$

where $I$ is the moment of inertia of the ball relative to the centre of mass, equal to $\frac{2}{5}mr^2$, and $\vec{\omega}$ is the angular velocity vector: its length is equal to the angular speed of rotation, its direction is the direction of the axis of rotation, and its sense is given by the right-hand screw rule.

Newton's second law for rotational motion has the form

$$\frac{\mathrm{d}\vec{L}}{\mathrm{d}t} = \vec{M},$$

where $\vec{M}$ is the resultant torque; in the case of many forces $\vec{F}_i$ acting on a given object it is equal to

$$\vec{M} = \sum_i \vec{r}_i\times\vec{F}_i,$$

where $\vec{r}_i$ is the vector starting at the point relative to which we calculate $\vec{M}$ and ending at the point of application of the force $\vec{F}_i$.

Above, $\times$ is the vector product; we have: $\left|\vec{a}\times\vec{b}\right| = |\vec{a}|\cdot\left|\vec{b}\right|\,|\sin\theta|$, where $\theta$ is the angle between the vectors $\vec{a}$ and $\vec{b}$; the vector $\vec{a}\times\vec{b}$ is perpendicular to $\vec{a}$ and $\vec{b}$, and its sense is given by the right-hand screw rule (we rotate from $\vec{a}$ to $\vec{b}$). The usual rule for differentiating a product holds for the vector product: $\frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}t}\left(\vec{a}\times\vec{b}\right) = \frac{\mathrm{d}\vec{a}}{\mathrm{d}t}\times\vec{b} + \vec{a}\times\frac{\mathrm{d}\vec{b}}{\mathrm{d}t}$

problems.title: Problem 2
problems.problem:
Problem 2 [20 points]

Consider the following model of an underwater geyser.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/physics-olympiads-bank/main/images/poland-2023-2-fig1.png

At a depth $h$ below the surface of a very shallow lake, in the rocks, there is a cave (a reservoir) completely filled with water. The rocks surrounding the reservoir have temperature $T_{\mathrm{s}}$. These rocks heat the water in the reservoir and at a certain moment it begins to boil. The water vapour completely pushes the water out of the channel connecting the cave with the lake, and then a sudden evaporation of part of the water in the reservoir occurs, visible as an eruption of the geyser.

The air pressure just above the surface of the lake is $p_0$, and the temperature of the water in the lake is $T_{\mathrm{j}}$. The height of the reservoir is much smaller than $h$. The volume of the channel connecting the cave with the lake is negligibly small compared with the volume of the reservoir, but it is wide enough not to resist the escaping vapour. During the eruption, water from the lake does not flow into the channel. Take into account that the density of the vapour is much smaller than the density of water. Assume that only vapour escapes from the geyser.

a) What must the temperature $T_{\mathrm{s}}$ be for the described phenomenon to be able to occur?

b) Assuming that during the eruption of the geyser a mass $m$ of water vapour escapes from it, determine the minimum amount of water accumulated in the cave under consideration just before the eruption of the geyser.

Neglect the heat supplied to the water during the eruption.

c) After the eruption the pressure in the reservoir drops and the water from the lake fills the reservoir again. Knowing that the time interval between eruptions is $\Delta t$, determine the average power of the heat supplied to the water.

The pressure of saturated vapour at temperature $T$ is, in the situation under consideration, to a good approximation equal to

$$p_{\mathrm{w}}(T) = p_0\,\mathrm{e}^{\frac{L_{\mathrm{m}}}{R}\left(\frac{1}{T_0}-\frac{1}{T}\right)},$$

where $R$ is the universal gas constant, $L_{\mathrm{m}}$ the molar heat of vaporisation of water at pressure $p_0$, and $T_0$ the boiling point of water at pressure $p_0$. Assume that the density of water does not depend on temperature and is equal to $\rho$. Assume also that the specific heat of water does not depend on temperature (in the range of temperatures occurring) and is equal to $c_{\mathrm{w}}$.

The molar mass of water is $M_{\mathrm{w}}$, the gravitational acceleration $g$.

Give the numerical results taking $h = 200\ \mathrm{m}$, $L_{\mathrm{m}} = 41\ \mathrm{kJ/mol}$, $T_0 = 373\ \mathrm{K}$, $R = 8.3\ \mathrm{J/mol{\cdot}K}$, $c_{\mathrm{w}} = 4.2\ \mathrm{kJ/(kg{\cdot}K)}$, $M_{\mathrm{w}} = 18\ \mathrm{g/mol}$, $g = 10\ \mathrm{m/s^2}$, $\rho = 1000\ \mathrm{kg/m^3}$, $m = 50\cdot10^{3}\ \mathrm{kg}$, $\Delta t = 1\ \mathrm{h}$, $T_{\mathrm{j}} = 293\ \mathrm{K}$, $p_0 = 1000\ \mathrm{hPa}$.

problems.title: Problem 3
problems.problem:
Problem 3 [20 points]

Two metal balls, each of radius $r$, are immersed in a large tank of salt water with conductivity $\sigma$ and permittivity $\epsilon$. The balls are connected to a battery by thin insulated wires, and their centres are a distance $d$ apart – see the figure. The voltage between them is $U$.

Assuming that the electric field outside the balls is the same as the field of point charges located at the centres of these balls, determine the current flowing through the water. Present the result to an accuracy of terms linear in $\frac{r}{d}$, i.e. in the form $A(1 + B\frac{r}{d})$, where $A$ and $B$ do not depend on $\frac{r}{d}$; this means neglecting terms of order $\frac{r^2}{d^2}$.

Give the numerical result for $U = 5\ \mathrm{V}$, $d = 0.1\ \mathrm{m}$, $r = 0.01\ \mathrm{m}$, $\sigma = 10^{-2}\ 1/(\Omega\cdot\mathrm{cm}) = 1.0\ /(\Omega\cdot\mathrm{m})$ $\epsilon = \epsilon_w\cdot\epsilon_0$ where $\epsilon_w = 80$, $\epsilon_0 = 8.85\cdot10^{-12}\ \mathrm{A^2{\cdot}s^4/(kg\cdot m^3)}$

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/physics-olympiads-bank/main/images/poland-2023-3-fig1.png

Notes:

1. The electric field due to a point charge $q$ located in a uniform medium of permittivity $\epsilon$ is given by the formula

$$\vec{E}(\vec{r}) = \frac{q}{4\pi\epsilon r^2}\,\frac{\vec{r}}{r},$$

where $\vec{r}$ is the vector from the charge to the point at which we examine the electric field.

2. The current density (i.e. the current per unit area) in a medium of conductivity $\sigma$, at a point where the electric field is $\vec{E}$, is equal to $\sigma\vec{E}$. This means that the current flowing through a small surface element $A$, perpendicular to $\vec{E}$, is equal to $\sigma AE$.

3. The walls and the surface of the water in the tank are at a much greater distance from the balls than the distance between them.

4. The electric field due to the wires can be neglected (this follows from the fact that they are thin).

5. For $|x| < 1$ the following holds:

$$(1+x)^{\alpha} = 1 + \frac{\alpha}{1!}x + \frac{\alpha(\alpha-1)}{2!}x^2 + \ldots$$

Problem 1 [20 points]

Inside a rectangular-cuboid tank with a flat horizontal bottom and width $L$, a uniform dam in the shape of a quarter-cylinder of radius $R$ and length $L$ has been placed along the side of width $L$ – see the figure. The depth of the water in the tank is also $R$ – see the figure:

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/physics-olympiads-bank/main/images/poland-2024-1-fig1.png

The dam is not fastened in any way – neither to the bottom nor at its ends, but the coefficient of friction between the material of the dam and the ground is non-zero and equal to $f$.

Find the minimum mass $m$ of the dam for which the water will neither shift it nor overturn it. The density of water is $\rho$, the gravitational acceleration is $g$.

We assume that the water does not seep under the base of the dam, but also that the dam does not stick to the ground by suction.

problems.title: Problem 2
problems.problem:
Problem 2 [20 points]

A solenoid has $N$ uniformly and densely wound turns, length $L$ and radius $r$, where $L\gg r$. In a plane perpendicular to the axis of the solenoid there is a non-conducting, uniform ring of inner radius $R_1$, outer radius $R_2$ ($L\gg R_2>R_1>r$) and mass $m$. The ring is equidistant from the ends of the solenoid, is uniformly charged with charge $Q$ and can rotate freely about its axis, which coincides with the axis of the solenoid.

At the instant $t=0$ the ring is not rotating. Find the angular velocity of rotation of the ring at the instant $t=T$, if a time-dependent current $I(t)=I_0\cdot t/T$ flows through the solenoid, where $I_0$ is a constant.

Neglect the magnetic field produced by the ring and the electrostatic charge induced by it in the circuit of the solenoid. Assume that the system is in vacuum.

The moment of inertia of a uniform disc of mass $M$ and radius $R$ about its axis is $MR^2/2$.

problems.title: Problem 3
problems.problem:
Problem 3 [20 points]

The newly founded company "Relax on your way to Mars" intends to produce recreational modules for spacecraft.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/physics-olympiads-bank/main/images/poland-2024-3-fig1.png

Diagram of the module. The water stream is shown in the frame co-rotating with the module.

[Labels in the figure: wewnętrzna powierzchnia modułu = inner surface of the module; kierunek obrotu modułu = direction of rotation of the module; woda = water; oś obrotu = axis of rotation; strumień wody ze zraszacza = water stream from the sprinkler.]

Such a module has the shape of a hollow cylinder of inner radius $R$. During the journey, when the rocket engines are switched off, the cylinder rotates about its axis at such a rate that the effective gravitational acceleration on the inner surface equals $g$. This inner surface is covered with a thin layer of soil on which grass grows. The grass is watered by sprinklers placed at ground level, fed from a water tank located on the axis of rotation. The air pressure inside the module and in the very small space "above" the water (i.e. right next to the axis of rotation) is equal to the Earth's atmospheric pressure $p_0$. The only cause of the flow of water to the sprinkler, and then of its outflow from it, is the "artificial gravity" caused by the rotational motion of the module.

Consider a stream of water emerging in the plane perpendicular to the axis of rotation at an angle $\alpha$ with respect to the ground, where $\alpha=0$ means outflow of the water in the direction of rotation of the cylinder. We assume that just past the outlet of the opening, all volume elements of the water move with the same velocity and in the same direction.

Assuming that there are no energy losses – neither during the flow of the water to the sprinkler nor after the water leaves the sprinkler – find the distance (measured along the inner surface of the cylinder) and the maximum height (measured as the distance along the radius from the ground) reached by the considered stream of water. Assume also that the speed of the water flow in the pipes connecting the tank with the sprinkler is much smaller than the speed of the water flowing out of the sprinkler. The mass of the outflowing water is much smaller than the mass of the station.

problems.title: Problem 1
problems.problem:
Problem 1 [20 points]

A space station orbits a certain spherical dwarf planet of mass $M$ along an elliptical orbit with pericentre $r_{\mathrm{p}}$ and apocentre $r_{\mathrm{a}}$. The station consists of two modules: 1 (of mass $m_1$) and 2 (of mass $m_2$), the astronauts being in module 1 (their mass is included in the mass of this module). The crew of the station has mutinied, and its aim is to eject module 2 in such a way that module 1, which they occupy, moves away from the planet beyond the practical range of its gravitational field (formally – to an infinitely large distance, of course over a very long time). The modules are separated by the explosion of charges located between them. The energy of the explosion is $E_{\mathrm{w}}$, and half of this energy is converted into the kinetic energy of the modules.

Find the minimum value of the energy $E_{\mathrm{w}}$ that makes the described manoeuvre possible. Assume that the direction in which module 2 is ejected can be controlled arbitrarily, and moreover that the ejection can take place at any point of the orbit. The duration of the ejection of the module is so short that during the ejection the influence of the gravity of the planet can be neglected, but long enough that the astronauts come to no harm from the action of a large g-force. The mutual gravitational interaction of the modules and the gravitational field produced by other celestial bodies should be neglected. Neglect the mass of the explosive charges compared with the masses of the modules. Neither the station as a whole nor the modules after separation rotate.

Give the numerical result when this dwarf planet is Ceres of mass $M=9.4\cdot10^{20}\,\mathrm{kg}$, and $m_1=1.0\cdot10^{5}\,\mathrm{kg}$, $m_2=4.0\cdot10^{5}\,\mathrm{kg}$, $r_{\mathrm{p}}=1.0\cdot10^{6}\,\mathrm{m}$, $r_{\mathrm{a}}=5.0\cdot10^{6}\,\mathrm{m}$. The gravitational constant is $G=6.67\cdot10^{-11}\,\mathrm{N\cdot m^2/kg^2}$.

problems.title: Problem 2
problems.problem:
Problem 2 [20 points]

A driver was driving a car at night along a straight road. At a certain moment he heard a short sound signal of frequency $f$, coming from a direction making an angle $\alpha$ with the direction of travel. The driver immediately strained his eyes and saw straight ahead (along the road) the lights of a locomotive passing over a level crossing. The driver knows that in this area the railway track is perpendicular to the road, the trains here travel at constant speed, and the locomotives emit a sound signal of frequency $f_0$. He also knows that the speed of sound in air is $v_{\mathrm{d}}$.

The driver immediately began to brake, moving with uniformly decelerated motion with an acceleration of magnitude $a$, as a result of which he stopped just in front of the tracks.

Find the distance of the locomotive from the car at the moment the car stops.

Give the numerical result for $\alpha=10^{\circ}$, $f_0=400\,\mathrm{Hz}$, $f=460\,\mathrm{Hz}$, $v_{\mathrm{d}}=340\,\mathrm{m/s}$, $a=5\,\mathrm{m/s^2}$.

Neglect the linear dimensions of the locomotive and of the car. The day was windless and the area flat.

problems.title: Problem 3
problems.problem:
Problem 3 [20 points]

A very long (i.e. of length much greater than its radius), uniform, rigid, hollow tube with thin walls and radius $R$ lies on a horizontal ground. The tube is cut by a horizontal plane parallel to the plane of the ground, at such a distance from it that the surface of the upper part of the tube is a fraction $x$ of the whole surface of the tube. A uniform current of total intensity $I$ flows through the upper part of the tube, along its axis, and a uniform current of total intensity $-I$ through the lower part. The mass of the tube per unit length is $\lambda$. Find the minimum current $I_{\min}$ above which the upper part of the tube will rise above the lower part.

Neglect the forces associated with the connecting wires. The gravitational acceleration is $g$, and the magnetic permeability of vacuum is $\mu_0$.

problems.title: Problem 1
problems.problem:
Problem 1 [20 points]

A uniform ball of mass $M$ and radius $r$ rests on a flat, horizontal ground. A small ball of mass $m$ and negligibly small radius is dropped onto the ball. The velocity of the small ball just before the collision is vertical and has magnitude $v_0$; the collision takes place at height $h$ above the ground ($h>r$). We consider only the situation in which, after the collision, the small ball rises, its maximum height during the motion being $H$ ($H>h$) above the ground.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/physics-olympiads-bank/main/images/poland-2026-1-fig1.png

Find the velocity of the centre of the large ball after the collision. Give the numerical result for $r=8\,\mathrm{cm}$, $h=15\,\mathrm{cm}$, $H=20\,\mathrm{cm}$, $M=3\,\mathrm{kg}$, $m=0.2\,\mathrm{kg}$, $v_0=5\,\mathrm{m/s}$, and the gravitational acceleration $g=9.81\,\mathrm{m/s}$.

Assume that the collision between the balls lasts a very short time, the surfaces of the balls are smooth, and the friction between them is zero. The coefficient of friction between the large ball and the ground is so large that this ball does not slip on the ground either during the collision or after it. Moreover, the large ball is in contact with the ground all the time; it does not bounce off it. There is no air resistance. The moment of inertia of a uniform ball about an axis through its centre is $I=2Mr^2/5$.

Note: it cannot be assumed that the collision is elastic.

problems.title: Problem 2
problems.problem:
Problem 2 [20 points]

A spherical planetoid of radius $R$ has been discovered in which, under a very thin rocky surface, there is an incompressible liquid of density $\rho$, and at the centre there is a spherical, spherically symmetric rocky core of radius $r_1$. A spherical probe of mass $m$ was immersed in the liquid to the maximum possible depth, i.e. down to the rocky core; the pressure measured by the probe at this depth is $p_1$. The dependence of the volume of the probe on the pressure $p$ is given by the formula $V=V_0(1-\alpha p)$, where $V_0$ and $\alpha$ are positive constants.

a) Find the minimum work that must be done in pulling the probe out of the liquid filling the planetoid by means of a weightless, thin, flexible and inextensible rope.

b) Find the mass of the rocky core.

The volume and the mass of the probe are much smaller than, respectively, the volume and the mass of the liquid. Neglect the gravity of other celestial bodies. The pressure at the surface of the liquid, i.e. just below the rocky layer, is much smaller than $p_1$ (practically equal to 0) and does not change while the probe is being pulled out.

In cases a) and b) find the numerical results for $R=4.00\cdot10^{5}\,\mathrm{m}$, $r_1=2.00\cdot10^{5}\,\mathrm{m}$, $p_1=3.00\cdot10^{7}\,\mathrm{Pa}$, $\rho=1000\,\mathrm{kg/m^3}$, $m=10\,\mathrm{kg}$, $V_0=1.05\cdot10^{-2}\,\mathrm{m^3}$, $\alpha=6.00\cdot10^{-9}\,/\mathrm{Pa}$. The gravitational constant is $G=6.67\cdot10^{-11}\,\mathrm{m^3/(kg\cdot s^2)}$.

problems.title: Problem 3
problems.problem:
Problem 3 [20 points]

Consider $N$ rigid, thin, long wires, parallel to one another, which – when no current flows – form the $N$ lateral edges of a regular prism. The distance between neighbouring edges is $d$, see the figure (it corresponds to the special case $N=6$). A current $I_k=I_0\cos(\omega t+2k\pi/N)$ flows through wire $k$ (where $k=1,2,\ \ldots,N$), where $I_0$ (the current amplitude) and $\omega$ (the angular frequency) are constants and $t$ is time.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/physics-olympiads-bank/main/images/poland-2026-3-fig1.png

The wires are mounted elastically, so that they can be displaced radially (change their distance from the axis of the prism), but they cannot move in the direction perpendicular to the radial one. Displacing a wire from the edge of the prism by a distance $x$ requires a force $Kx$ per unit length of the wire, where $K$ is a constant. The mass of each wire per unit length is $\lambda$.

a) For what angular frequency $\omega$ does resonance occur?

b) Assuming that there is no resonance, find the mean radial displacement from the edge of the prism and the amplitude of the radial oscillations of each of the wires a long time after the current is switched on. Take a positive value of this displacement to correspond to an increase of the distance of the wire from the axis of the prism.

Assume that the displacement of a wire from the edge of the prism is small compared with $d$ – so small that even in the case of resonance this displacement does not affect the forces of mutual interaction of the wires.

Notes:

If a periodic force $F=F_0\cos(\Omega t)$ acts on a harmonic oscillator of mass $m$ and spring constant $k$, then after a long time, for $\Omega^2\neq k/m$, the oscillator will oscillate according to the formula $x=A\cos(\Omega t)$, where $A=F_0/(k-m\Omega^2)$ (these are the so-called steady-state oscillations).

Note that the quantity $I_0\cos(\omega t+\alpha)$ can be interpreted as the $x$-component of a vector of length $I_0$ rotating in the $xy$ plane with angular velocity $\omega$, where at the instant $t=0$ this vector makes an angle $\alpha$ with the $x$ axis.

Assume that the magnetic interactions are as if the system were in vacuum. Neglect the influence of the supply wires – those bringing the current in and taking it out (they are not shown in the figure; the mountings of the wires are not shown either).
